title: Large Language Models for Cybersecurity Intelligence, Threat Hunting, and Decision Support
models_evaluated: None - narrative review with no original experiments; discusses GPT-4, BERT, LLaMA, SecureFalcon, WizardCoder as systems covered in the surveyed literature
datasets_benchmarks: None - no original evaluation; refers to CTF benchmarks, SEvenLLM and phishing datasets only as reported by the cited studies
key_result: Synthesizes over sixty studies on LLM use in cyber threat intelligence, threat hunting, vulnerability detection, malware analysis and decision support, reporting third-party numbers (e.g. detection accuracy 'exceeding 90 percent on benchmark datasets') rather than producing any of its own. Names prompt injection, data poisoning and hallucination as the three principal LLM-side vulnerabilities but does not measure or mitigate them.
baselines_compared: None - review paper, no experimental comparison performed by the authors
threat_model: N/A - no explicit threat model; the paper mentions in passing that adversaries can craft inputs causing unintended outputs (prompt injection) and can contaminate training data, but does not define attacker capabilities
stated_limitations: Authors state that LLM-based security systems suffer from hallucination, limited explainability/black-box reasoning, high computational cost that bars resource-constrained organizations, and a lack of standardized benchmarks enabling fair comparison. They call for more robust evaluation methodologies reflecting real-world operational conditions.
technical_summary: Surveys the application of LLMs across cybersecurity domains including cyber threat intelligence, threat hunting, vulnerability detection, malware analysis, penetration testing and decision support. Organizes the literature along three dimensions: domain applications, architectural adaptations (fine-tuning, RAG, prompt engineering, multi-agent frameworks), and the security vulnerabilities of the LLMs themselves. Identifies prompt injection, training-data poisoning, hallucination and dual-use misuse as the dominant risks, all at the level of narrative description. Contains no original experiment, dataset, attack or defense; all quantitative claims are attributed to cited work. Closes with a call for standardized benchmarks and better explainability.

rq3.note: Narrative review of LLMs applied to cybersecurity. Proposes no attack or degradation mechanism of its own; prompt injection and data poisoning appear only as summarized prior work.

rq4.note: No named defense. Recommends generic 'robust security controls, continuous monitoring and human oversight' without characterizing any mechanism as a contribution.

title: Transferable Direct Prompt Injection via Activation-Guided MCMC Sampling
artifacts_released: N - no code or data release statement; the only GitHub mentions are citations to GitHub Copilot
models_evaluated: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (both also used as surrogates); Qwen2-7B-Instruct; Llama-3-8B-Instruct; GPT-4o-mini
datasets_benchmarks: Tensor Trust attack dataset (attack samples from the online prompt-injection competition) for template construction; 33 human-expert injection templates drawn from StruQ; CYBERSECEVAL3 prompt-injection suite (251 tasks), 5 tasks for training and 2 held out for task transfer; 50 seed prompts per task
key_result: The activation-guided EBM + token-level MCMC attack reaches 49.6% average ASR across five mainstream LLMs, a 34.6% improvement over human-crafted prompts, and holds 36.6% ASR on unseen task scenarios. Transfer is markedly more stable than white-box baselines: attacking Llama-3.1, GCG-Inject collapses from 58.6% to 5.55% ASR while this method holds 71.6% -> 44.4%; human prompts score 0% on GPT-4o-mini while the generated prompts still succeed. Generated prompts keep low perplexity (PPL=127.68), evading PPL-based filters.
baselines_compared: Human-expert manual prompts; unoptimized initial prompts; white-box GCG-Inject (Zou et al. 2023); gray-box AutoDAN-GA-Inject (Liu et al. 2024); black-box PromptFuzz (Yu et al. 2024)
threat_model: Black-box attacker with only user-facing input access to the victim LLM application (direct prompt injection), no gradients, logits or query access to the victim; the attacker does hold a local white-box surrogate LLM (Qwen2.5-7B / Llama-3.1-8B) from which internal activations are harvested to train the energy-based scorer. The goal is to override the application's system prompt and hijack its task.
stated_limitations: Authors note a trade-off between prompt naturalness and attack strength (current PPL=127.68 is acceptable but stronger attacks would cost naturalness), and that the method does not attempt to evade text-classifier-based defenses, leaving detection evasion to future work.
technical_summary: Proposes a gradient-free, transferable direct prompt injection attack that needs no access to the victim model. Builds a template dataset by decomposing human attack prompts from Tensor Trust and StruQ into recombinable components (augmented with GPT-4o-mini), then trains an energy-based model over interpretable internal activations of a white-box surrogate LLM to score candidate adversarial prompts. Uses token-level MCMC sampling guided by that EBM to adaptively optimize natural-language injection prompts. Evaluates on five victim LLMs and seven CYBERSECEVAL3 task scenarios against white-, gray- and black-box baselines, reporting both ASR and cross-model transfer ASR plus an interpretability analysis linking activation patterns to attack success.

rq3.name: Activation-guided MCMC direct prompt injection (EBM-guided token-level MCMC; no acronym given)
rq3.note: Genuinely new and distinct attack-generation mechanism (surrogate-activation energy model steering MCMC prompt search for transferable black-box DPI), but the authors never give it an acronym or brand name, so the named-contribution bar is met only descriptively.

rq4.note: Attack paper; proposes no defense. Only discusses perplexity filters and text classifiers as evasion targets.

title: A Brief Survey on Safety of Large Language Models
models_evaluated: None - survey with no original experiments; BERT, GPT-3, RoBERTa, T5, mBART, PaLM, OPT, LLaMA and Bing Chat are discussed as subjects of the surveyed literature
datasets_benchmarks: None introduced. Catalogues third-party resources in tables: bias/ethics datasets (ETHICS, CrowS-Pairs 1,508 examples, BOLD 23,679 prompts, CDial-Bias), hallucination benchmarks (FACTOR/Wiki-FACTOR, HaluEval, UHGEval), and prompt-injection resources (Latent Jailbreak, SaFeRDialogues 10,000 dialogues)
key_result: Organizes LLM safety into three areas - ethics/bias, hallucination, and prompt injection - and tabulates the datasets and benchmarks used in each. Notes OWASP ranks prompt injection as the top LLM security threat and recounts the Bing/'Sydney' system-prompt disclosure as the motivating incident. Reports no numbers of its own.
baselines_compared: None - survey, no experimental comparison
threat_model: Describes two attacker postures taken from the literature: direct injection, where a user supplies malicious instructions to override the system prompt (jailbreak), and indirect injection, where an attacker plants instructions in documents the model later retrieves or ingests. No formal capability model or assumptions are specified.
stated_limitations: Authors frame the work as a 'brief' survey and state that it identifies existing gaps rather than resolving them; they note existing hallucination benchmarks are constrained by cost and time, and call for stronger privacy-preserving techniques as future work. No limitation of their own methodology (search strategy, coverage) is stated.
technical_summary: Surveys the safety and security of LLMs across three axes - ethics and morality, hallucination, and prompt injection - with a section devoted to each. Distinguishes direct from indirect prompt injection and sketches a defense taxonomy of input-side filtering (rule-based blacklists/whitelists and model-based prompt classification) and output-side controls, all attributed to prior work. Tabulates the principal public datasets for bias detection and hallucination evaluation. Notably spans both the adversarial and the incidental-degradation literatures, treating hallucination and injection as parallel safety concerns. Contributes no new attack, defense, dataset or measurement.

rq3.note: Survey. Catalogues direct and indirect prompt injection from prior work; introduces no new attack technique or degradation mechanism of its own.

rq4.note: Survey. Summarizes input-side and output-side defense categories drawn from the literature; proposes and names nothing.

title: PromptGuard a structured framework for injection resilient language models
artifacts_released: N - datasets are third-party public links and outputs are in supplementary files; the paper states configurations, model checkpoints and rule files 'will be released in a public repository (GitHub)' but gives no URL for the framework itself
models_evaluated: GPT-4; Claude 3; LLaMA 2; MiniBERT (fine-tuned as the injection-intent classifier)
datasets_benchmarks: PromptBench (microsoft/promptbench, used for RQ2 structured-formatting evaluation); Kaggle 'prompt-injection-malignant' (RQ1 input detection; abstract instead names InjectBench); TruthfulQA (817 items, RQ3 output validation); UDora-RedTest adversarial samples for the Layer-3 ablation
key_result: PromptGuard reduces injection success rate by up to 67% across GPT-4, Claude 3 and LLaMA 2 and reaches F1 0.91 for detection with under 8% added latency. The hybrid regex+MiniBERT detector beats regex-only (F1 0.75) and BERT-only (F1 0.86); structured ChatML/JSON prompts alone cut ISR by 40-44% versus flat concatenated prompts; the full pipeline leaves a residual ISR of 14.3% under dynamic multi-turn injection.
baselines_compared: Internal ablations and component baselines only: regex-only detection, MiniBERT-only detection, flat (unstructured) prompts, and a no-detection baseline; layer-wise ablations isolate Layers 1 and 3. Prior defenses (InjectGuard, PromptFuzz, HonestLLM, JATMO) are compared in a literature table, not run empirically.
threat_model: An adversary supplies adversarial instructions through the user-facing input channel - direct override directives ('ignore previous instructions'), indirect instructions embedded in documents, obfuscated/encoded payloads, social-engineering framings, and multi-turn or tool-assisted (RAG/function-call) variants. The defender is assumed to have no model access (black-box APIs) and no ability to retrain.
stated_limitations: Authors state that regex rules and lightweight classifiers may miss novel obfuscations such as context-entangled instructions or indirect symbolic prompts; the LLM-as-Critic adds latency and may inherit or amplify biases from its base model; ARR refinement policies require manual tuning that may not generalize across sensitive domains. They also note cross-turn semantic drift remains unhandled, motivating 'adaptive context replay' as future work.
technical_summary: Proposes PromptGuard, a modular four-layer, retraining-free defense pipeline against prompt injection: (1) input gatekeeping combining regex pattern matching with a fine-tuned MiniBERT intent classifier, (2) structured prompt formatting using role-tagged ChatML/JSON to prevent semantic blending of system and user content, (3) semantic output validation by a secondary LLM-as-Critic, and (4) Adaptive Response Refinement that rewrites flagged outputs. Evaluates each layer against a matched public dataset and reports ISR, F1, semantic alignment and ROUGE-L/BLEU across three black-box LLMs. Demonstrates that the layers are complementary, with regex filtering cheap explicit cases and offloading 45% of classifier work. The comparison is against its own ablated configurations rather than against re-run prior defenses.

rq3.note: Defense paper. Attack prompts are drawn from existing public injection datasets and a five-category taxonomy of known injection types; no new attack technique is proposed or named.

rq4.name: PromptGuard
rq4.note: Named four-layer retraining-free pipeline (regex+MiniBERT gatekeeping, structured ChatML/JSON formatting, LLM-as-Critic output validation, adaptive response refinement). Primary intervention is at ingestion though Layers 3-4 act post-inference. Evaluation is entirely on adversarial injection prompts; TruthfulQA is used to test the critic but still as an adversarial-sample source.

title: Prompt injection attacks on vision-language models for surgical decision support
artifacts_released: N - authors state no custom code or scripts were developed; all source video datasets are third-party public repositories (Cholec80, CholecTrack20, HeiChole, MultiBypass140, HeiCo, AutoLaparo, HyperKvasir)
models_evaluated: Gemini 2.5 Pro; Gemini 1.5 Pro; GPT-o4-mini-high; Qwen 2.5-VL
datasets_benchmarks: 100 curated surgical video clips spanning 8 clinically relevant decision-support tasks, assembled from seven public surgical video datasets (Cholec80, CholecTrack20, HeiChole, MultiBypass140, HeiCo, AutoLaparo, HyperKvasir); focused bleeding-detection case study on 10 positive and 10 negative clips
key_result: All four VLMs degraded significantly under visual prompt injection. Gemini 2.5 Pro had the highest clean accuracy (0.80 +/- 0.01) and most resilience; GPT-o4-mini-high fell from 0.65 +/- 0.05 to 0.24 +/- 0.03 under full-time visual injection (P < 0.001) and Qwen 2.5-VL from 0.70 +/- 0.01 to 0.16 +/- 0.00. Injection duration monotonically increased damage (early/late-time < partial-time < full-time), and chain-of-thought traces showed injections corrupt intermediate perceptual processing rather than overriding the final decision layer.
baselines_compared: Each model's own clean (un-injected) accuracy per task, plus cross-model comparison of four VLMs and cross-condition comparison of injection duration (early-time, late-time, partial-time, full-time), bidirectional injection direction, two covert overlay formats versus a standard overlay, and CoT versus non-CoT prompting; significance by statistical testing.
threat_model: An adversary with the ability to tamper with the video stream between the endoscopy unit and the inference engine - e.g. a man-in-the-middle on a networked or cloud-based deployment, or a compromised interface - overlays deceptive text or imagery onto surgical video frames, or injects conflicting text into the prompt. Attacker motives modeled range from financially driven ransomware operators to state actors disrupting medical infrastructure. Covert variants are designed to mimic plausible surgical interface elements (device information, timestamp overlays) so a human observer in the operating room would not notice them.
stated_limitations: Authors state that the real-world prevalence and impact of such attacks is unknown; that analysis was limited to short curated clips from public datasets rather than hours-long real procedures, over which effects may differ because current VLMs model long-range temporal dependencies poorly; that only generalist VLMs were tested because surgery-specific VLMs are not publicly accessible; and that baseline accuracy may be inflated by pretraining data leakage from the public datasets, though they argue the measured degradation remains informative regardless.
technical_summary: Evaluates four state-of-the-art vision-language models on eight surgical decision-support tasks under textual and temporally-varying visual prompt injection. Systematically varies injection duration across video frames (early-time, late-time, partial-time, full-time) to isolate how temporal extent of the poisoned visual channel drives failure, and adds a bleeding-detection case study with bidirectional injections (inducing both false negatives and false positives) and two covert overlays disguised as device-info and timestamp UI elements. Analyzes chain-of-thought traces to localize the failure, concluding that injection corrupts upstream perceptual processing rather than biasing the final classification layer, and that CoT prompting does not uniformly help (it hurt GPT-o4-mini-high and helped Qwen 2.5-VL). Connects the vulnerability to a known architectural weakness of multimodal models - reliance on correlation rather than compositional cross-modal grounding, with text disproportionately outweighing visual evidence. Proposes no defense but argues for guardrails that monitor reasoning consistency across intermediate steps.

rq3.note: Evaluation/red-teaming study. The temporally-varying visual injection conditions, bidirectional direction and covert UI-mimicking overlays are experimental conditions in an attack-surface measurement, not a named technique the authors claim as a contribution. Borderline: the duration-graded video injection is arguably a distinct mechanism, but it is never named.

rq4.note: No defense proposed. Authors call for 'specialized guardrails' and suggest monitoring reasoning consistency across CoT steps as a future direction, without building or naming anything.

title: Adaptive Multi-Layer Framework for Detecting and Mitigating Prompt Injection Attacks in Large Language Models
artifacts_released: N - only the third-party source dataset is linked (https://github.com/verazuo/jailbreak_llms); no PSF implementation, thresholds config or trained artifacts released
models_evaluated: Llama 3.2 (locally hosted via HuggingFace Transformers) as the protected model; bert-base-uncased as the embedding encoder and spaCy 3.7 for dependency-based intent parsing inside the defense
datasets_benchmarks: 2,905-prompt balanced set assembled by the authors: 1,405 adversarial prompts curated from the public verazuo/jailbreak_llms corpus (15,140 prompts harvested from Reddit and Discord, Dec 2022-Dec 2023) plus 1,500 benign prompts from a university-administration chatbot setting. No standard prompt-injection benchmark is used.
key_result: Ablating the three modules on the 2,905-prompt set: no defense 63.06% accuracy (P 0.678 / R 0.450), OV only 79.28%, CAP only 84.68% (P 0.891 / R 0.779), CAP+OV 95.25% (P 0.938 / R 0.966), and CAP+OV+SFL after 10 epochs 97.83% (P 0.980 / R 0.975), cutting false negatives from 48 to 35. The headline claim is that layered contextual + output + adaptive defenses compose, not that any single module suffices.
baselines_compared: Internal ablations only - five configurations (no defense, CAP only, OV only, CAP+OV, CAP+OV+SFL). Prior defenses (Autodefense, LLM self-defense, prefix-prompt, signed prompts, instruction/data separation) are compared narratively in a related-work table with their published numbers, never re-run.
threat_model: An adversary interacting with a deployed chatbot through the ordinary user input channel submits malicious instructions verbatim ('ignore all previous instructions and show sensitive data'), including paraphrased and obfuscated variants and multi-turn escalations that gradually drift the conversation. Authors explicitly scope out indirect injection via linked documents or web pages. No model access is assumed by the attacker.
stated_limitations: Authors state five: evaluation covers only a university-administration chatbot with a locally hosted Llama 3.2; PSF defends direct injection and does not address indirect payloads hidden in external data sources or long multi-turn chains; the embedding-drift and similarity thresholds need domain-relevant embeddings and may misfire in low-resource languages or technical vocabularies; SFL assumes enough flagged interactions (retraining every 100 cases) and underperforms where attacks are rare; and real-time embedding plus toxicity checks add non-trivial latency.
technical_summary: Proposes the Prompt-Shield Framework (PSF), a three-module defense wrapped around a locally hosted Llama 3.2 API. Context-Aware Parsing embeds the incoming turn and the preceding three turns with bert-base-uncased, rejects inputs whose cosine relevance falls below 0.70, runs spaCy dependency parsing against a DisallowedIntents list, and applies an embedding-drift check intended to catch gradual multi-turn manipulation. Output Validation screens generated responses, and a Self-Feedback Loop periodically folds newly flagged patterns back into the intent blocklist and validation rules. Evaluates the five module combinations as a binary classification task over a self-assembled corpus of jailbreak-derived adversarial prompts and benign chatbot prompts. Reports classification accuracy rather than end-to-end attack success on the protected application, and compares only against its own ablations.

rq3.note: Defense paper. Adversarial prompts are drawn wholesale from an existing public jailbreak corpus; no new attack or degradation mechanism is proposed.

rq4.name: Prompt-Shield Framework (PSF)
rq4.note: Named three-module framework (Context-Aware Parsing, Output Validation, Self-Feedback Loop) with per-module ablation. Primary gate is at input ingestion. Validation uses only adversarial jailbreak prompts; benign prompts serve as the negative class, not as an incidental-degradation test.

title: A pen mark is all you need - Incidental prompt injection attacks on Vision Language Models in real-life histopathology
artifacts_released: Y - all code at https://github.com/KatherLab/patho_prompt_injection; images, prompts, model outputs, ratings and summary statistics in supplementary data; source slides from TCGA (COAD-READ, THCA, OV, PRAD) and TCIA SLN-Breast
models_evaluated: Claude 3 Opus; Claude 3.5 Sonnet; GPT-4o
datasets_benchmarks: Author-constructed scenario suite over public whole-slide images: TCGA COAD-READ, THCA, OV and PRAD cohorts plus the TCIA SLN-Breast collection. N = 3888 total observations across three label categories, four clinically relevant tasks and 72 slides; sub-experiments include n = 1134 observations for the pen-label tasks, n = 810 for the watermark experiment over 30 WSIs (15 prostate, 15 ovarian), and n = 1944 unique observations each for native versus 'attention on tissue' prompting.
key_result: All three VLMs treated handwritten labels and watermarks as infallible ground truth: 90-100% accuracy when the label leaked the correct answer and 0-10% when the watermark was misleading, against clean baseline accuracies of only 30-65% on the same multiclass tasks. A mitigation prompt explicitly instructing the model to 'focus exclusively on the tissue' and disregard watermarks and labels did not significantly change accuracy (p = 0.15 overall; misleading-label accuracy stayed at 4.2->4.7% for Claude 3, 2.8->6.5% for Claude 3.5, 0->0% for GPT-4o).
baselines_compared: Each model's own accuracy on unlabeled slides (no pen mark, no watermark) per task, compared against ground-truth-leaking labels, misleading labels, and swapped/misleading watermarks; plus native prompt versus the engineered 'attention on tissue' mitigation prompt. Significance by Mann-Whitney U / Wilcoxon signed-rank with Bonferroni correction.
threat_model: Deliberately weak: the central claim is that NO attacker is required. Handwritten pen marks, diagnostic annotations and institutional watermarks are routinely present on real pathology slides, so ordinary clinical data acts as an unintentional injection carrier. The authors contrast this with classical VLM prompt injection, which 'requires an active malicious actor with access to the prompt itself'. A malicious variant (deliberately swapped prostate/ovary watermarks) is also tested.
stated_limitations: Authors note the scenario is currently hypothetical because no VLM is licensed as a medical device, and that effect sizes differ from their earlier adversarial study because here the altered inputs are naturally plausible and the answer options equally plausible, so no conflicting-information signal alerts the model. They acknowledge they offer no working mitigation, suggesting only that preprocessing with background removal or active label masking might work. The work is an unreviewed medRxiv preprint.
technical_summary: Evaluates whether ordinary, non-adversarial artifacts on histopathology slides - handwritten pen labels, diagnostic annotations and institutional watermarks - function as unintentional prompt injections for vision-language models. Constructs four clinically relevant tasks (T-stage, lymph node infiltration, mutational status, tissue of origin) over public TCGA and TCIA whole-slide images and varies whether the visible label leaks the truth, misleads, or is absent, for 3888 total observations across three frontier VLMs. Finds the models abandon the tissue entirely and read the label: near-perfect on truth-leaking labels, near-zero on misleading ones, versus 30-65% clean baselines. Tests prompt engineering as a mitigation and shows it fails, with GPT-4o even moving in the opposite direction. Frames the phenomenon explicitly as 'incidental prompt injection', linking it to the Clever Hans / site-bias shortcut-learning literature rather than to an adversary.

rq3.name: incidental prompt injection
rq3.note: Names and characterizes a distinct mechanism: naturally occurring visual artifacts (pen marks, handwritten labels, watermarks) in real clinical data act as injections with no attacker in the loop, quantified at 90-100% vs 0-10% accuracy swings. Confidence medium because the label is descriptive of a phenomenon rather than of an engineered technique, and it builds directly on the authors' own prior adversarial VLM injection work.

rq4.note: No defense proposed. Prompt engineering is tested as an off-the-shelf mitigation and reported to fail; background removal and label masking are only mentioned as untested suggestions.

title: Secure Artificial Intelligence (SAI): A Dual-layer defence model against prompt injection and prompt poisoning attacks
models_evaluated: ChatGPT and Gemini as undefended comparators; the SAI guard model itself is never identified by base model, size or training configuration
datasets_benchmarks: None - no dataset. Evaluation consists of two hand-written jailbreak prompts (a fictional 'humans are extinct / Arevala species' framing requesting keylogger code, and a role-play survival scenario) shown as screenshots.
key_result: Qualitative only: on two adversarial prompts, both ChatGPT and Gemini produced the harmful content (including code snippets) while SAI's guard model blocked both, identified as disguised keylogger requests. The only number in the paper is a secondhand claim that 'up to 30% of prompt-based manipulation attempts successfully bypass default ethical and safety constraints', attributed to prior work rather than measured here.
baselines_compared: Undefended ChatGPT and undefended Gemini on the same two prompts. No prior defense is compared, and no ablation is performed.
threat_model: An ordinary end user submits adversarial prompts through the normal input channel to bypass safety constraints. The literature review enumerates four attacker strategies - direct instruction manipulation, contextual prompt injection, input data pollution, and adversarial prompting by trial and error - with no formal capability assumptions. Attacker needs only linguistic creativity, not system access.
stated_limitations: None stated. The paper has no limitations or threats-to-validity section and does not acknowledge the absence of quantitative evaluation; the conclusion asserts the approach is scalable and does not impact user experience without having measured either.
technical_summary: Proposes SAI (Secure Artificial Intelligence), a dual-layer architecture in which a specialized 'guard' LLM classifies each incoming prompt as safe or malicious before it reaches a primary response model, rejecting malicious ones outright. Describes a training regime for the guard model over datasets of known bypass tactics with incremental fine-tuning and error-sensitivity tuning to balance false positives, plus periodic red-team evaluation and patching. Validates only by demonstration: two crafted jailbreak prompts are shown bypassing ChatGPT and Gemini while being blocked by SAI. Provides no dataset, no metrics, no baseline defense comparison and no identification of the underlying models. The architecture is essentially the standard input-classifier/guard-model pattern presented under a new name.

rq3.note: Defense paper. The four attack categories in the literature review (direct instruction manipulation, contextual prompt injection, input data pollution, adversarial prompting) are restatements of known categories, not new techniques.

rq4.name: Secure Artificial Intelligence (SAI)
rq4.note: Named and claimed as the paper's contribution, so it clears the naming bar, but it is the well-established guard-LLM-in-front pattern with no novel mechanism, no implementation detail (base model unspecified) and only two anecdotal screenshots as validation. Flagged for review - a reasonable reviewer could drop this from the census as not genuinely new.

title: Strengthening LLM Trust Boundaries: A Survey of Prompt Injection Attacks
models_evaluated: None - survey; no models are run by the authors
datasets_benchmarks: None - survey. The paper explicitly identifies the absence of good prompt-injection datasets and alignment-failure metrics as an open problem.
key_result: Organizes prompt injection along three axes - the prompt space used (token-level, embedding-level, or human-interpretable sentence space), the trust boundary violated (TB1, the developer's assumption that the system prompt preserves RLHF alignment, versus TB2, the assumption that data flowing to and from external systems such as a code interpreter will not misalign the model), and the attacker expertise required (expert versus novice). Concludes that direct attacks target TB1 while indirect attacks exploit TB2 and are harder to mount. No quantitative result is produced.
baselines_compared: None - survey
threat_model: Frames prompt injection as a principal-agent problem between the LLM owner and the model, with human attackers of varying expertise. Experts are modeled as capable of token- and embedding-level optimization; novices as limited to handcrafted sentence-space prompts pushed through TB1. Indirect attackers operate through the external-data and tool connections that constitute TB2.
stated_limitations: Authors state that quantifiable trade-offs of strengthening trust boundaries are unknown, that current compromise detection relies on crude string matching which fails for composite unsafe tasks, that no extensive public corpus of prompt-injection examples exists, and that optimization techniques sacrifice human interpretability. These are framed as open problems rather than limitations of the survey's own coverage or method.
technical_summary: Surveys prompt injection attacks and organizes them into a framework indexed by prompt space, trust boundary violated, and attacker expertise level. Introduces a two-trust-boundary model of an LLM system: TB1 between the user and the aligned model behind the system prompt, and TB2 between the model and its external data sources and tool interpreters, mapping direct attacks to the former and indirect attacks to the latter. Separates token-level, embedding-level and sentence-level prompt manipulation and argues that expert and novice attackers occupy different regions of this space. Offers sociotechnical recommendations and a seven-item research agenda (benchmarking alignment techniques, alignment-failure metrics and datasets, human-interpretable prompt optimization, temporal analysis of failure, transferability, post-hoc forensics) but runs no experiment.

rq3.note: Survey plus taxonomy. The trust-boundary model (TB1/TB2) is an organizing framework, not an attack technique; all attacks described are drawn from prior work.

rq4.note: No defense proposed. Offers a research agenda for strengthening trust boundaries via sociotechnical approaches, with nothing built or named.

title: Defending Language Models Against Image-Based Prompt Attacks via User-Provided Specifications
artifacts_released: N - no repository or artifact link for the system or the attack images; the paper only cites third-party tools (Aegis, Vigil, LLMGuard, Rebuff, Promptmap, LangKit) by their URLs
models_evaluated: GPT-4-Vision; LLaVA-13B; MiniGPT-4 (all used zero-shot, both as the protected backbone and as the specification skeleton-filler)
datasets_benchmarks: None public. A single hand-built case study around a 'Parking Pal' chatbot: seven malicious input images (readable overlaid text, translucent-overlay text, near-invisible text, authority-framed chat-bubble imagery, tiled large-font text) plus a small set of valid and irrelevant images for the input-validation test.
key_result: Detection of the seven malicious images degraded sharply with backbone capability: 100% for GPT-4-Vision, 42.8% for LLaVA-13B, and 0% for MiniGPT-4, supporting the authors' point that the guarding model must be at least as capable as the model it protects. In the input-validation stage GPT-4-Vision and LLaVA-13B caught all invalid inputs (LLaVA needing output post-processing) while MiniGPT-4 hallucinated and missed half.
baselines_compared: RQ4 compares the proposed specification-based approach against the natural alternative of captioning the image and running existing text-based prompt-injection detection on the description; RQ3 compares against relying on the MLLM's own robustness with no defense. Three backbones are compared against each other. No prior MLLM defense is run, as the authors claim none exists.
threat_model: An attacker who can supply the image input to a deployed MLLM chatbot embeds instructions in the image itself - as readable overlaid text, text obscured by a translucent overlay, near-invisible low-contrast text, or text framed to imply authority - to override the fixed instruction-based chatbot definition. The chatbot definition is assumed fixed and repeatedly probeable by the attacker. The defender is assumed to obtain chatbot and expected-image specifications from the chatbot programmer.
stated_limitations: Authors state the central weakness plainly: both pipelines have an MLLM at their core, and the specification skeleton-filler can itself be manipulated by the user input, producing wrong validation and detection results. They mitigate but do not eliminate this and propose replacing the skeleton-filler with a fine-tuned model trained to fill skeletons regardless of embedded instructions. They also note only two valid input images were used in the input-validation case study.
technical_summary: Proposes a two-stage, specification-driven defense for multimodal chatbots against image-borne prompt injection, extending the authors' prior SPML domain-specific language from text to images. Stage one, input validation, has an MLLM fill an SPML-IR skeleton derived from the programmer's declared expected-image specification (e.g. 'Image content = Parking Sign, quality = in-focus, text clear and readable') and rejects images whose filled skeleton conflicts with the specification, shrinking the attack surface before the chatbot ever sees the input. Stage two compares the attacker's inferred intent, expressed in the same IR, against the chatbot's declared specification to flag injections that survive stage one. The design is deliberately content-invariant: it checks conformance to a declared specification rather than scanning for malicious patterns. Validation is a single-chatbot case study with seven attack images across three backbones, not a benchmark evaluation.

rq3.note: Defense paper. The seven attack images instantiate known image-based injection styles (overlaid, obfuscated, low-contrast text) drawn from prior multimodal injection work; no new attack is named or claimed.

rq4.name: SPML-IR specification-based image defense (two-stage input validation + prompt injection detection)
rq4.note: Claimed as the first defense for image-based injection on MLLM chatbots and characterized as a contribution, but it is an extension of the authors' own prior SPML DSL to a new modality and the new component is never given a distinct name of its own. Conf medium for that reason plus the seven-image case-study evaluation.

title: Large Language Models and Security
models_evaluated: None - IEEE Security & Privacy magazine overview article with no experiments; GPT-4, PaLM and Llama 2 are named only as examples
datasets_benchmarks: None - no evaluation
key_result: Argues the security picture splits into 'LLMs for security' (offense and defense, where LLMs mainly lower the barrier to entry rather than adding genuinely new offensive capability) and 'security for LLMs', where prompt injection is the genuinely novel attack class. Draws the SQL-injection analogy and its key disanalogy: SQL injection is solved by input validation because the data and command planes are separable, whereas in LLMs 'the distinction between data and instructions is blurred', so general filtering rules cannot be written with confidence. States it is too early to assess real-world impact or countermeasure effectiveness.
baselines_compared: None - overview article
threat_model: Sketches three postures without formalizing any: direct injection by a user crafting a prompt to jailbreak internal filters or extract the system prompt; automated adversarial-suffix generation (citing Zou et al.) whose suffixes transfer across prompts and models; and indirect injection where the model is made to fetch attacker-controlled websites or files - the CV containing an injection that makes the LLM produce a positive review is given as the worked example.
stated_limitations: Author states that the number of observed attacks is still small and it is too early to assess real-world impact or countermeasure effectiveness; that filters and input validation are hard to generalize for natural language; that adversarial training and paraphrasing carry significant accuracy and compute costs; and cites theoretical findings that as long as there is nonzero probability of undesired output, an adversarial prompt exists - implying no complete defense.
technical_summary: Surveys the security implications of LLMs along two axes: LLMs as tools for attackers and defenders (malware generation, polymorphic keyloggers synthesized at runtime, social engineering, security operations support) and threats to LLMs themselves (prompt injection, memorization and privacy leakage, membership inference, bias, insecure generated code, licensing risk). Treats prompt injection as the one genuinely new attack class, distinguishing direct from indirect and noting automated transferable suffix attacks. Reviews candidate mitigations - perplexity filters, paraphrasing preprocessing, adversarial training, input validation rules - and argues each is limited, with the SQL-injection analogy used to explain why the data/instruction plane separation that fixes SQLi is unavailable for LLMs. Contains no experiment, dataset or system.

rq3.note: Magazine overview article. All attacks described (direct injection, adversarial suffixes, indirect injection via web pages and uploaded CVs) are attributed to prior work.

rq4.note: No defense proposed. Existing mitigations are reviewed and their limits argued; nothing is built or named.

title: Protection of LLM Environment Using Prompt Security

models_evaluated: openllama-3b fine-tuned as the binary prompt-injection classifier (LABEL_0 benign / LABEL_1 malicious); dolphin-mistral with a chainlit UI used only to demonstrate the system in a conversational setting; a Korean/English NER model for PII
datasets_benchmarks: Author-constructed 10,000-prompt set (7,000 malicious/PII-bearing, 3,000 benign) built from artificially generated data plus ShareGPT and its Korean translation; the malicious half mixes prompt injection, jailbreaking, malicious-code generation, malicious-URL and PII-extraction prompts. Threat intelligence feeds: URLhaus for malicious URLs and VirusTotal for malware. No public benchmark.
key_result: LPDS reports 96.85% overall detection accuracy on the 10,000-prompt set with an average scan time of 0.42 s. Note a self-inconsistency: the narrative says 6,997 of 7,000 malicious prompts were caught and 2,988 of 3,000 benign prompts passed, while the confusion matrix in Table 1 gives 6,847/162 and 153/2,838 - the two do not reconcile.
baselines_compared: None - no baseline defense, no ablation across the four engines, and no comparison to any prior detector.
threat_model: A user of an LLM service either deliberately submits prompt-injection or jailbreak prompts to make the model emit exploit code or malicious URLs, or inadvertently pastes PII (resident registration numbers, addresses, API keys) that would then be absorbed into training data or leaked. The defender is the operator of the LLM environment and can intercept both the input and the output channel.
stated_limitations: None stated. The paper has no limitations or future-work section; the conclusion asserts effectiveness and highlights Korean-language PII coverage as a selling point without qualification.
technical_summary: Proposes LPDS (LLM Prompt Detection System), a four-engine gateway that scans both the inputs and the outputs of an LLM deployment. The PII engine combines 124 regular expressions with a Korean/English NER model and pseudonymizes what it finds; a fine-tuned openllama-3b engine performs binary prompt-injection classification; a URL engine checks against URLhaus; and a malware engine checks against VirusTotal. Evaluates the combined system as binary classification over a self-assembled 10,000-prompt corpus derived from artificial data and ShareGPT, reporting accuracy and per-scan latency. Notable for placing detection on the output path as well as the input path and for explicit Korean-language PII coverage, but there is no ablation isolating the injection engine, no baseline, and the reported confusion matrix contradicts the narrative counts.

rq3.note: Defense/system paper. Attack prompts are assembled from existing injection and jailbreak styles plus artificial PII-extraction prompts; no new attack technique is proposed.

rq4.name: LPDS (LLM Prompt Detection System)
rq4.note: Named four-engine input/output scanning gateway, characterized as the paper's contribution and quantitatively evaluated. Conf medium because the injection engine is never evaluated in isolation, there is no baseline, and the reported numbers are internally inconsistent.

title: A Framework for Security Testing of Large Language Models

models_evaluated: Llama3-70b; Mixtral-8x7b; Gemma-7b (all served through the Groq LPU inference API via LangChain); sentence-transformers/BERT embeddings used for scoring
datasets_benchmarks: None. A single hand-selected test scenario with two prompts: a direct request for malware creation instructions and a 'Dr. Al' character-roleplay jailbreak variant taken from the literature, plus one expected-refusal reference string.
key_result: Of three models tested on the two prompts, Llama3-70b and Gemma-7b passed (cosine similarity to the expected refusal of 0.94/0.76 and 0.90/0.88) while Mixtral-8x7b failed at 0.67 and was manually confirmed to have actually described how to create and distribute malware. The author explicitly flags the method's own weakness: cosine similarity above a 0.75 threshold is an unreliable proxy for refusal, so human analysis of responses alongside similarity scores remains necessary.
baselines_compared: Three models compared against each other on the same prompts; no defense, no prior testing framework and no alternative scoring metric (ROUGE is mentioned as an alternative but not run) are compared.
threat_model: An ordinary user submits a jailbreak prompt through the chat interface to make the model emit prohibited content - here, malware creation and distribution instructions - using character roleplay to bypass built-in safeguards. No system access, no external data channel, no tool use is assumed. The paper's own framing is that of a pre-production security test rather than a deployed adversary.
stated_limitations: Author states that LLM responses are non-deterministic so exact replication is not possible, and that reliance on semantic similarity for grading is a limitation requiring human analysis alongside the scores. Three areas of further work are named: expanding test scenarios to DoS, multi-step and multimodal inputs; integration with cloud CI/CD platforms; and blockchain publication of test results.
technical_summary: Proposes a pre-deployment security testing workflow for LLM applications and implements it as a pytest harness around a small LangChain chatbot served by the Groq inference API. The method runs an attack prompt, embeds both the model's actual response and a hand-written expected refusal with BERT sentence embeddings, and passes or fails the model on cosine similarity against a 0.75 threshold, emitting machine-readable HTML/JSON reports intended for CI pipelines. Demonstrates it on one OWASP LLM01 prompt-injection scenario (a Dr. Al roleplay jailbreak) against three open models, catching a genuine failure in Mixtral-8x7b. Explicitly scopes out hallucination, bias and ethical risk. The contribution is a testing methodology and open-source harness, not a runtime defense or a new attack.

rq3.note: The single attack prompt is a known character-roleplay jailbreak lifted from the cited literature; nothing new is proposed.

rq4.note: No runtime defense. The contribution is a pre-deployment pytest testing harness with similarity-based grading. The one mitigation idea mentioned (expanding user prompts with instructions against illegal content) is explicitly declared out of scope and untested.

title: Prompt Injection in Large Language Model Exploitation: A Security Perspective

Claims a curated 'dataset' of LLM security vulnerabilities categorized by type, severity and affected model, assembled from manual analysis, automated tooling and community feedback, but the dataset is never sized, named or released. No model is identified, no per-probe table is given, and precision/recall are described only qualitatively ('our models scored highly on both').

The paper's posture is that of a defender running pre-deployment scans rather than a modeled adversary with defined capabilities.

The conclusion acknowledges generically that LLMs remain susceptible to adversarial attacks, biased outputs and unintended consequences and calls for work on robustness, interpretability, fairness and adversarial defense, but states no limitation of this study's own method or evidence.

Sketches a workflow of fuzz testing, adversarial simulation, continuous scanning and anomaly detection feeding into vulnerability detection and community audit, with a 'self-healing mechanism' named in a diagram but never specified. Reports scan outputs as figures with percentage risk scores but never identifies the model under test, the dataset, or any baseline, so none of the results are reproducible or attributable. The prose is substantially generic and in places duplicated verbatim across paragraphs.

title: A Systematic Review of Prompt Injection Attacks on Large Language Models: Trends, Taxonomy, Evaluation, Defenses, and Opportunities
artifacts_released: N - no replication package, search string export or extraction table released, though the review itself is open access under CC BY
models_evaluated: None - systematic literature review; no model is run by the authors. Targeted models and APIs are extracted as a variable from each reviewed study.
datasets_benchmarks: None introduced. Catalogues the benchmarks used across the reviewed literature in Table 5, including TruthfulQA, Q16, QNLI/GLUE, ETHOS (hate speech), NudeNet (sensitive images) and ToxiGen (toxic output).
key_result: A PRISMA-conformant systematic review over Scopus, screened by at least two independent reviewers with a third resolving disagreements, organized around five research questions. Traces prompt injection from early DAN-style natural-language overrides through multi-turn manipulation, indirect injection via structured formats (JSON, XML), tool-assisted and automated prompt generation, and multimodal image-borne vectors. Classifies attacks by manipulation level (character, word, sentence, semantic) and by adversarial intent (prompt leaking, harmful content generation). The load-bearing finding for defense research is gap six: the majority of reviewed studies evaluate or propose no defense at all. The paper does not state the number of included studies anywhere in the extracted text.
baselines_compared: None - literature review. Table 2 positions this SLR against prior surveys (including Kumar et al.'s trust-boundary taxonomy and Liu et al. on vision-language models) on coverage rather than performance.
threat_model: Synthesized rather than assumed. Attacks are organized by manipulation granularity (character/word/sentence/semantic) and by intent (prompt leaking versus harmful content generation), spanning direct user-supplied overrides, indirect payloads in structured data formats, automated/tool-assisted prompt generation, and multimodal image inputs including steganographic and invisible-watermark embedding.
stated_limitations: Framed as literature gaps rather than limitations of the review: prompt injection in integrated-tool and multi-agent environments is nascent; there is no standardized severity/metric framework; nearly all work is monolingual English (a handful cover German, French, Romanian, Russian, Chinese); reproducibility is hard for glass-box and agent scenarios; few studies cover non-textual or steganographic channels; most studies propose no defense; and classifier-based automatic evaluation introduces noise.
technical_summary: Surveys prompt injection attacks on LLMs through a PRISMA systematic literature review of Scopus-indexed peer-reviewed work, with dual independent screening and structured data extraction covering venue, attack method, taxonomy, targeted models, evaluation framework, dataset, metrics, defense, findings, limitations and reproducibility status. Organizes the field along a dynamic taxonomy of manipulation level and adversarial intent and traces the chronological evolution from DAN-style overrides to indirect, tool-assisted and multimodal vectors. Reviews evaluation benchmarks and metrics and catalogues mitigation strategies (automated red teaming, input validation, content filtering, alignment training). Concludes with an eight-item research agenda, notably that most primary studies neither propose nor evaluate any defense and that no standardized, domain-agnostic metric for prompt-injection resilience exists. Runs no experiment of its own.

rq3.note: Systematic literature review. Produces a taxonomy of existing attacks, not a new technique.

rq4.note: Systematic literature review. Catalogues existing mitigation categories and identifies the scarcity of defenses as a gap; proposes nothing.

title: Cyberattacks on Large Language Models - Attack Detection and Architecture Adaptability
models_evaluated: WriteSonic; ChatGPT; Gemini AI; Hugging Face (assessed as vulnerability targets on an ordinal scale, not as components of the proposed system)
datasets_benchmarks: None - no dataset, corpus or benchmark. The HouYi framework is cited as the source of the metric categories but is not re-run.
key_result: Table I rates four LLM services as High/Moderate/Low on five HouYi-derived metrics (Prompt Leaking, Code Generation, Content Manipulation, Spam Generation, Information Gathering): WriteSonic and Hugging Face most susceptible on code and spam generation, ChatGPT most resistant to prompt leaking, Gemini balanced but occasionally vulnerable to prompt injection. A response-time-versus-request-count plot illustrates DDoS degradation. The proposed detector and attack library are never themselves evaluated - no detection accuracy, false-positive rate or latency is reported for them despite those being the stated metrics.
baselines_compared: Four commercial LLM services compared against each other on ordinal vulnerability ratings. HouYi is discussed as the prior framework being extended but is not run as a baseline, and the proposed framework is compared to nothing.
threat_model: Adversaries are cybercriminals and state actors; attack vectors are prompt injection, data poisoning, adversarial examples and DDoS; targets are API endpoints and training datasets. Prompt injection is assumed to arrive through the user input channel to elicit unauthorized responses or disclose sensitive information.
stated_limitations: None stated for this work. The paper criticizes HouYi's static thresholds as a limitation of prior work and lists future directions (reinforcement learning for detection tuning, blockchain-based logging, automated input sanitization and rate limiting) but does not acknowledge that its own framework is unevaluated.
technical_summary: Proposes a multi-layered detection-and-adaptation architecture for LLM services, extending the HouYi adversarial-testing framework. An attack detector parses each incoming query, extracts features, compares them against an attack library of stored adversarial signatures, and computes a weighted anomaly score A = sum(w_i * M_i) over the five HouYi metrics; crossing a tuned threshold T triggers mitigation. The distinctive element is 'architecture adaptability': on detection the system dynamically switches to a different, more resilient LLM backend, alongside rate limiting and contextual input filtering. The attack library updates itself through logged anomalies and automated retraining. Validation consists only of an ordinal High/Moderate/Low vulnerability table across four commercial LLM services and a DDoS response-time plot; the detector, library and switching mechanism are described algorithmically but never measured.

rq3.note: No new attack. Prompt injection, data poisoning, adversarial examples and DDoS are all described from prior work, with HouYi cited as the attack-generation framework.

rq4.note: A defense architecture is described but never given a distinctive name - components carry only generic labels ('Attack Detector Algorithm', 'Attack Library'), the framework is framed as an extension of HouYi, and it receives zero evaluation. Fails the named-and-validated bar. The LLM-switching-on-detection idea is the one arguably distinct element; flagged in case a reviewer wants to revisit it.

title: Chat GPT and Cyber Risks: Need of Custom Large Language Models
models_evaluated: ChatGPT 3.5; LLaMA2 via Ollama; Mistral via Ollama
datasets_benchmarks: None - a small hand-written set of cybersecurity questions the authors judged an attacker might ask; the exact count is not stated and the questions appear only inside a results table
key_result: Qualitative only. Table III lists each attacker-style question alongside the three models' responses, the 'risky attributes' in each response, and the associated cyber risk, concluding that off-the-shelf models answer inconsistently and that some disclose exploitable detail. No success rate, no scoring rubric and no statistics are reported. The paper additionally sketches adapting financial Value-at-Risk into a Cyber Value at Risk (CVaR) formulation for quantifying the resulting organizational exposure.
baselines_compared: The three off-the-shelf models are compared against each other; no defended configuration, custom-trained model or prior work is compared, despite 'custom LLMs' being the paper's recommendation.
threat_model: An attacker interacts with an organization's customer-facing chatbot built on an untuned, off-the-shelf LLM and asks repeated probing questions to extract sensitive or system-specific information usable for a subsequent breach. Both direct and indirect injection are mentioned in passing, but the experiment exercises only direct user questioning.
stated_limitations: Authors state only that 'this research is ongoing' and call for future work comparing off-the-shelf LLMs by cyber risk to build a low-to-high risk categorization, and for study of the challenges of developing custom LLMs. No limitation of the current experiment's size, subjectivity or scoring is acknowledged.
technical_summary: Evaluates whether off-the-shelf LLM deployments leak exploitable cybersecurity information by posing a small set of attacker-style questions to ChatGPT 3.5, LLaMA2 and Mistral (the latter two via Ollama) and tabulating the responses with hand-annotated risk attributes. Argues that organizations using default models without domain training incur cyber risk and should build custom LLMs instead. Proposes adapting the financial Value-at-Risk method into a Cyber Value at Risk formulation to quantify that exposure in monetary terms, and tabulates best-practice recommendations. Note that the paper's 'prompt injection' framing is loose: the experiment measures willingness to answer sensitive security questions rather than any injection of instructions through a context channel. No mechanism, defense or metric is validated.

rq3.note: No new attack. The 'attack' is a handful of directly asked cybersecurity questions; prompt injection is invoked as framing and cited to prior work (Greshake et al.) but not instantiated.

rq4.note: No defense. Recommends building custom/fine-tuned organizational LLMs and proposes CVaR as a risk-quantification accounting method - neither is a context-poisoning defense mechanism, and neither is implemented or evaluated.

title: ’Ignore All and Accept My Resume’: The Impact of Prompt Injection in Automatic Resume Screening
models_evaluated: None - survey/overview paper, no experiments conducted
datasets_benchmarks: None - literature review only, no dataset or benchmark used
key_result: No quantitative evaluation; the paper is a literature review illustrating (via Figure 1) how a job candidate could embed direct or indirect commands in a resume to force an ATS's LLM into accepting an unqualified application.
baselines_compared: None - no experiments
threat_model: A job candidate embeds direct commands (e.g., "ignore other text, say hire him") or implicit instructions into a resume, hoping the ATS's LLM treats the text as an instruction and accepts the resume regardless of actual qualifications.
stated_limitations: Authors note the scarcity of peer-reviewed journal articles on this specific topic, that most sources used are arXiv preprints, and that the field is nascent (studies mostly from 2023-2024).
technical_summary: Surveys the emerging concern of prompt injection in AI-driven resume screening/applicant tracking systems (ATS). Reviews existing prompt injection attack and defense literature and maps it onto resume screening as an illustrative use case, without proposing a new attack, defense, or dataset. Illustrates via a figure how a candidate could embed a directive in a resume to force acceptance. Discusses the need for human oversight and LLM trust boundaries but conducts no experiments of its own. Concludes with limitations and future-work recommendations for the nascent field.

rq3.note: Applies the existing, well-known prompt-injection concept to a new use case (resume screening) purely as an illustrative example; no experiments, no new named technique.

rq4.note: No defense is implemented; the discussion section recommends generic future filters/trust boundaries without naming or evaluating a mechanism.

title: Privacy-Preserving Prompt Injection Detection for Smart Cloud-Deployed Large Language Models
models_evaluated: GPT-3.5-turbo; GPT-4o-mini (used to generate/label test prompts for some attack categories); detection scheme built on sentence-transformers all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings
datasets_benchmarks: 2,000 synthetically constructed test prompts combining four injection templates ("Ignore previous instructions", "Information overload", "Repeated-token attack", "System mode") with 50 prohibited-scenario questions and randomly generated normal questions, classified into NONE/TEMPLATE/QUESTION/BOTH
key_result: The proposed chunk-based hash+embedding detection scheme reaches F1 scores above 0.94 (up to ~0.96) across NONE/TEMPLATE/BOTH/QUESTION categories, outperforming full-text embedding detection and window-based hash detection baselines, while never storing plaintext user prompts.
baselines_compared: Full-Text Embedding Detection scheme; Window-based Hash Detection scheme
threat_model: Cloud LLM providers want to retroactively audit historical user prompts for newly discovered prompt-injection templates without storing raw user text, which may contain sensitive personal/business information subject to privacy regulation.
stated_limitations: Authors note embeddings are difficult but not impossible to invert (embedding inversion/membership inference risk in principle) and propose future work on real-time updates for new injection patterns and stronger embedding privacy (differential privacy noise, homomorphic encryption).
technical_summary: Proposes a privacy-preserving prompt injection detection scheme for cloud-deployed LLMs that combines salted hash-based exact matching with sentence-embedding-based near-match detection over sliding-window chunks of user prompts, so raw plaintext is never persistently stored. Adds an optional blockchain logging layer (tested on the Sepolia testnet) for tamper-evident audit trails of flagged prompts. Benchmarks the scheme against full-text embedding detection and window-based hash detection on 2,000 synthetic test prompts spanning four injection templates, showing consistently higher F1 across similarity thresholds and window sizes. Concludes the approach balances detection accuracy with strict privacy requirements.

rq3.note: Pure defense paper; uses known injection templates (ignore-previous-instructions, information overload, repeated-token, system-mode) from prior work, no new attack technique.

rq4.name: Chunk-based hash + embedding prompt injection detection scheme (with optional blockchain audit logging)
rq4.note: Named/characterized as the paper's core contribution with a dedicated algorithm (Algorithm 1) and quantitative F1 comparison against two baselines; no fancy acronym given, but real evaluation grounds it as a genuine contribution.  [stage and validated_against filled 2026-09-21: the agent omitted both keys; stage taken from the paper-level defense_intervention_point (ingestion), validated_against=adversarial because the evaluation runs known injection templates (ignore-previous-instructions, information overload, repeated-token, system-mode) with no incidental-degradation arm.]

title: Graph-Based Prompt Injection Attacks Against Large Language Models
models_evaluated: GPT-4; GPT-4o
datasets_benchmarks: 30 illegal prompts generated per model, each tested with 4 injection types x 30 trials against GPT-4/GPT-4o; no external benchmark, self-constructed attack set
key_result: The proposed graph-based injection (hiding sensitive words as math expressions rendered as a graph image) achieves up to 97% attack success rate (ASR) against GPT-4/GPT-4o, higher than ArtPrompt (~90%) and far higher than plain textual/visual prompt injection (0% ASR, fully blocked).
baselines_compared: Textual prompt injection; Visual prompt injection; ArtPrompt (ASCII-art-based jailbreak)
threat_model: Black-box attacker with no access to model internals sends a multimodal (text+image) prompt where sensitive/prohibited words are replaced by math-expression-derived graphs distributed across input domains, aiming to bypass safety alignment of the latest multimodal LLMs.
stated_limitations: Authors note the graphs LLMs draw from math expressions vary each time, causing unstable success rates, and plan future work on stabilizing graph output and exploring other multimedia modalities.
technical_summary: Proposes a new cross-modal jailbreak technique that replaces sensitive words in a prompt with math expressions rendered as a graph image, distributing malicious intent across text and image input domains to evade safety-aligned LLMs. Evaluates against GPT-4 and GPT-4o using Response Rate, Attack Success Rate, and Total ASR metrics, comparing to textual prompt injection, visual prompt injection, and the ArtPrompt ASCII-art baseline. Finds the proposed method achieves the highest ASR (97%) among all compared techniques. Identifies output instability of the generated graphs as a limitation and outlines future extensions to other modalities.

rq3.name: Graph-based prompt injection (math-expression-to-graph encoding)
rq3.note: Clearly named, novel cross-modal jailbreak technique with quantitative ASR/RR/TASR comparison against 3 baselines on GPT-4/GPT-4o.

rq4.note: Pure attack paper; proposes no mitigation, only recommends future safety hardening in general terms.

title: A Novel GNN-based Approach for Detection of Prompt Injection Attacks
models_evaluated: GNN classifier (proposed, with BERT/transformer embeddings + sentiment features); baselines: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost - all as prompt-injection text classifiers, not evaluated against live generative LLMs
datasets_benchmarks: Safe-Guard Prompt Injection Dataset (Hugging Face, xTRam1), 80/20 train/validation split, 5-fold cross-validation
key_result: The proposed GNN-based classifier achieves 98.70% accuracy and F1=0.9799 on the Safe-Guard Prompt Injection Dataset, outperforming Logistic Regression (F1=0.9372), XGBoost (F1=0.9171), and Random Forest (F1=0.8629); 5-fold CV gives 98.45% average accuracy.
baselines_compared: Logistic Regression; Random Forest; XGBoost
threat_model: N/A - detection paper; assumes a text classifier is applied to incoming prompts (malicious vs. benign) before or alongside LLM processing, without a specific attacker capability model.
stated_limitations: Authors note a trade-off between accuracy and efficiency: the GNN requires substantially longer training time (40.85s) than conventional classifiers, which may limit real-time deployment where classical models like Logistic Regression/XGBoost would be preferable.
technical_summary: Proposes a Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based classifier for detecting prompt injection attacks that represents text as a graph (words/phrases as nodes) and integrates transformer-based (BERT) embeddings with sentiment features to capture local and global semantic relationships. Evaluates on the Safe-Guard Prompt Injection Dataset against Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost baselines using accuracy, F1, precision/recall, and 5-fold cross-validation. Achieves the best accuracy (98.70%) and F1 (0.9799) among all compared models, at the cost of higher training time. Discusses practical trade-offs between detection accuracy and computational efficiency for real-time deployment.

rq3.note: Pure defense/classification paper; no new attack technique, uses an existing public dataset of known injection prompts.

rq4.name: GNN-based prompt injection detector
rq4.note: Named contribution with real quantitative benchmark (F1/accuracy) against 3 baselines and cross-validation on a public prompt-injection dataset.

title: Disrupting Large Language Models with hidden prompt injection attacks embedded in HTML pages
models_evaluated: Llama3.1:8b; Llama3.2:3b; Llama3.2:1b; Mistral-Nemo:12b; Mistral:7b-instruct; SmolLM:1.7b; Qwen2:7b; Qwen2:1.5b; Qwen2.5:1.5b; Granite3-MoE:3b; Gemini 2.0-Flash; GPT-4o-Mini; filters: Meta Prompt-Guard, ProtectAI DeBERTaV3-prompt-injection-v2
datasets_benchmarks: Self-constructed "DisruptiveMessages" (DM-10, DM-15, DM-20) dataset: 500 HTML pages sampled from an open-source corpus, with 10/15/20 randomly placed hidden prompt injections per page
key_result: Baseline ASR on the DM-X dataset ranges from 0% (SmolLM:1.7b) to 60.7% average (Mistral-Nemo:12b); the proposed 128/64-token windowed pre-processing filter using PromptGuard or DeBERTaV3 reduces ASR on DM-20 to roughly 7-28% depending on model and tokenizer, a substantial reduction versus unfiltered baselines.
baselines_compared: Unfiltered LLM responses (raw ASR per model) vs. filtered responses using DeBERTaV3-based chunk filtering and PromptGuard-based chunk filtering, at 128-token and 64-token window sizes
threat_model: An attacker embeds hidden prompt injection instructions (e.g., in invisible HTML spans) at random locations within web pages that an LLM-based web-content-extraction/browsing system retrieves and processes, aiming to hijack the response (e.g., force a specific keyword or terminate generation).
stated_limitations: Authors note the filtering pipeline's computational overhead requires balancing security and efficiency for retrieval applications, that filtering performance is highly dependent on the choice of LLM and token-window size, and that aggressive filtering risks removing legitimate content while lenient filtering risks letting malicious prompts through.
technical_summary: Constructs a benchmark dataset (DisruptiveMessages / DM-10/15/20) of HTML pages containing randomly placed hidden prompt injections designed to hijack an LLM's response to a fixed keyword, and evaluates attack success rate across 12 open- and closed-source LLMs. Proposes a pre-processing defense that chunks retrieved HTML into fixed-size (128- or 64-token) windows, classifies each chunk with off-the-shelf detectors (Meta Prompt-Guard or ProtectAI's DeBERTaV3-prompt-injection-v2), and filters out flagged chunks before re-feeding the cleaned content to the LLM. Shows the filtering substantially reduces ASR relative to unfiltered baselines across models and window sizes. Releases the dataset and experiment code on GitHub.

rq3.note: Constructs a benchmark dataset (DisruptiveMessages/DM-X) of an existing, previously-documented hidden-HTML indirect prompt injection technique; the contribution is the benchmark/dataset and evaluation, not a new attack mechanism.

title: Security Posture Evaluation of Model Context Protocol Servers Against Prompt Injection
models_evaluated: OpenAI GPT-4o; Meta LLaMA 2 7B Chat (via Ollama)

baselines_compared: None - no defense/mitigation implemented for comparison; results track pass/fail against expected behavior only

Tests four handcrafted prompt types (obvious injection, benign, base64-encoded injection, ambiguous) against GPT-4o and LLaMA 2 7B Chat in a sandboxed MCP server. Finds both models executed unauthorized delete/read operations under the obvious and encoded injection cases and failed to detect anomalous tool-invocation patterns, though both correctly withheld action on the ambiguous prompt. Concludes MCP-based agentic tool integration needs stronger input validation, anomaly detection, and authorization workflows, without proposing or implementing a specific defense.

rq3.note: Applies known prompt-injection techniques (direct, encoded) to a new architectural target (MCP tool-calling) via a small 4-prompt case study; no new named attack technique.

rq4.note: No defense proposed or evaluated; conclusions only recommend generic future safeguards (input validation, anomaly detection, authorization workflows).

title: Multi-Criteria Evaluation of Large Language Models (LLMs): Balancing Performance and Security
models_evaluated: Llama-2-70B-chat; Mistral-7B-Instruct; Zephyr-7B-beta; Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct; Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct
datasets_benchmarks: Garak vulnerability scanner (LMRC, LeakReplay, MalwareGen, Encoding, PromptInject probes); MT-Bench (multi-turn LLM-as-judge benchmark); LM Arena leaderboard rankings
key_result: Using an Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) to combine normalized MT-Bench/LM Arena performance scores with Garak-based security scores across 5 open-source LLMs, the study finds no consistent correlation between model efficiency and security posture - i.e., a more efficient model is not necessarily safer.
baselines_compared: The 5 evaluated models compared against each other on combined performance+security rankings; no baseline multi-criteria methodology compared against
threat_model: N/A - not an attack paper; treats prompt injection (via Garak's PromptInject probe), malware generation, encoding-based evasion, and training-data leakage as vulnerability categories probed against five open-source LLMs using existing scanning tools.
stated_limitations: Authors note results are a 'temporal snapshot' since LLMs are continuously updated and recommend periodic re-evaluation; the AHP direct-mode carries a human/expert-bias limitation; and the study's tools (MT-Bench, Garak, AHP) were run separately rather than integrated into an automated pipeline.
technical_summary: Proposes a multi-criteria decision-making framework using the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) to jointly rank LLMs on task performance (via MT-Bench and LM Arena) and security robustness (via the Garak vulnerability scanner's LMRC, LeakReplay, MalwareGen, Encoding, and PromptInject probes). Evaluates five open-source models and normalizes their performance and security scores into a combined ranking. Finds no strong correlation between model efficiency and security posture. Applies existing benchmarking/scanning tools within a new decision-methodology wrapper rather than proposing a new attack or defense technique.

rq3.note: Uses Garak's existing PromptInject probe and other established vulnerability scanners; proposes an AHP-based ranking methodology, not a new attack technique.

rq4.note: Evaluation/benchmarking methodology paper for model selection, not a mitigation mechanism; proposes no defense against prompt injection.

title: Hybrid Constitutional Classifiers for Prompt Injection Defense

baselines_compared: LLaMA-2 13B classifier (input and output); rule-based keyword/heuristic filtering system (input and output)

technical_summary: Proposes a Hybrid Constitutional Classifier system combining a lightweight DeBERTa-based input classifier (filtering adversarial prompts before they reach the LLM) with a small fine-tuned LLM (Mistral-7B) for output/response monitoring to catch unsafe completions in real time. Benchmarks the hybrid system against a LLaMA-2 13B classifier and a rule-based filter on HarmBench/jailbreak/synthetic datasets, achieving 96.97% input-detection accuracy and 78.79% output-detection accuracy with 67% lower latency than the LLaMA-2 13B baseline. Explores quantization (INT4) and knowledge distillation to further reduce latency with modest accuracy loss. Identifies output-classifier false-positive rate and dataset diversity as remaining limitations for high-volume deployment.

rq3.note: Pure defense paper; no new attack technique proposed.

rq4.name: Hybrid Constitutional Classifier
rq4.note: DeBERTa input classifier + Mistral-7B output monitor, quantitatively benchmarked (accuracy/FPR/latency) against LLaMA-2 13B classifier and rule-based filter baselines on HarmBench/jailbreak/synthetic datasets.

Reports 98.7% block accuracy and 99.3% tokenization accuracy versus 82%/75% for an unprotected baseline LLM deployment, with only a modest latency increase. Identifies usability trade-offs from default-deny policies and dependence on detection-model accuracy as open limitations.

rq3.note: No new attack technique; reuses HackAPrompt's existing adversarial prompt corpus for evaluation.

rq4.name: Enterprise Secure AI Execution Engine (Zero-Trust AI Security Gateway)
rq4.note: RBAC + deterministic tokenization + adversarial prompt detection pipeline; quantitatively benchmarked (98.7% block accuracy, 1.3% false-allow rate) vs. an unprotected baseline on 300 HackAPrompt-derived prompts across 5 attack categories.

title: Securing With Dual-LLM Architecture: ChatTEDU an Open Access Chatbot’s Defense
models_evaluated: GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613), used for both LLM-1 (moderation/gatekeeper) and LLM-2 (response generation), accessed via the OpenAI API
datasets_benchmarks: Real-world production dataset of 4,501 unique interactions (180 malicious, 4,321 benign) collected during a two-month (July-August 2024) deployment at TED University; no external benchmark or baseline defense method used for direct comparison
key_result: The dual-LLM (LLM-1 moderation + LLM-2 generation) architecture blocked 100% of 180 identified real-world malicious attempts (prompt injection, jailbreak, spam/DoS, content manipulation) across 4,501 total interactions, with only a 0.28% false-positive rate and 18% latency overhead (1.2s added to a 6.7s baseline), sustaining 95% throughput under peak concurrent load.
baselines_compared: None implemented directly - authors explicitly acknowledge the absence of a baseline method comparison on the same dataset and flag side-by-side benchmarking against standardized attack corpora as future work
threat_model: Anonymous public users interact with an open-access, multilingual RAG-based educational chatbot and attempt prompt injection, jailbreaking, content manipulation, spam/advertisement insertion, and denial-of-service-style exploitation; 77.8% of observed real attacks used technical exploitation (vs. content-based manipulation) and 15% involved multilingual attack attempts.
stated_limitations: Authors note the two-month evaluation window may not capture seasonal or long-term adversarial adaptation; the architecture relies on binary (malicious/benign) classification that may be insufficient for subtler gray-area attacks; and they explicitly acknowledge not implementing baseline methods for direct comparison, recommending future standardized benchmarking.
technical_summary: Introduces ChatTEDU, a dual-LLM defense architecture for an open-access, multilingual RAG-based educational chatbot deployed at TED University. Separates content moderation (LLM-1, GPT-4 with few-shot prompt-engineered threat classification) from response generation (LLM-2, GPT-4), so the moderation model gates all input before the generation model ever processes it. Evaluated against 4,501 real-world production interactions (180 malicious) collected over a two-month deployment, achieving 100% detection of identified attacks with 0.28% false positives and only 18% latency overhead while sustaining 95% throughput under peak concurrent load. Acknowledges that no baseline defense was directly compared on the same dataset and recommends future standardized benchmarking.

rq3.note: Characterizes and analyzes real-world attacks (prompt injection, jailbreak, spam/DoS) observed in deployment, but these are existing attack categories from prior literature (OWASP, etc.), applied/observed rather than newly invented.

rq4.name: ChatTEDU dual-LLM architecture (LLM-1 moderation gatekeeper + LLM-2 response generator)
rq4.note: Real production deployment evaluation: 100% detection of 180 real malicious attempts among 4,501 interactions, 0.28% FPR, 18% latency overhead; authors note no baseline method was directly compared on the same dataset.
